messages:
maria.dev: Hey folks — hitting TLS cert errors from the Node SDK when running behind our corporate proxy in CI. Works on my laptop but CI containers get `Error: self signed certificate in certificate chain`. Node 18, sdk v1.4.2. Any recommended env vars or CA bundle placements?

aj: What base image/os is CI using? Curl against the endpoint from inside the CI container — does it succeed? Quick debug: you can temporarily set `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` to see if it's the CA, but don’t use that in prod. Also try `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/etc/ssl/certs/company.crt`.

maria.dev: CI is Ubuntu 22.04 image. `curl https://api.redwood.example` from container gives: "curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: self signed certificate in certificate chain" — so yeah it's the CA.

sophie: For Python clients it's `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` or `SSL_CERT_FILE` (OpenSSL). For requests: `requests.get(url, verify='/etc/ssl/certs/company.crt')` or set `export REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE=/etc/ssl/certs/company.crt` in the environment before running tests. For pip installs in CI, you can `pip --cert /etc/ssl/certs/company.crt install ...`.

tim.ops: Corporate MITM is almost certainly inserting a trusted root. You need to add the company root CA into the container's system trust store as part of your CI image. On Debian/Ubuntu: `cp company.crt /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/company.crt && update-ca-certificates`. For Alpine: `cat company.crt >> /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` then `update-ca-certificates`.

leo: A few Node-specific notes: Node uses OpenSSL for trust lookup. `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` points to a PEM file of extra root certs. Example Dockerfile snippet:```\nCOPY company.crt /tmp/company.crt\nRUN cp /tmp/company.crt /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/company.crt && update-ca-certificates && \\n    export NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/usr/local/share/ca-certificates/company.crt\n```\nAlso if you’re using a custom https.Agent in the SDK, make sure you aren't overriding the default `ca` list. If you do need to pass a CA to gRPC in Node: `const creds = grpc.credentials.createSsl(fs.readFileSync('company.crt'))`.

maria.dev: That’s helpful — thanks. Two follow-ups: 1) any gotchas for streaming responses (SSE/ws) behind MITM? 2) customer asked about mTLS between our private runtime and their proxy — how should SDKs handle client certs?

sophie: For streaming (SSE/websocket) there’s no extra TLS step beyond the initial handshake; if the cert chain is trusted the stream will work. Where it breaks is usually in the container missing the CA or a proxy refusing upgraded connections. Look at proxy logs.

sophie: For mTLS the SDK should support passing a client cert/key. Python requests: `requests.get(url, cert=("/path/to/cert.pem","/path/to/key.pem"), verify='/path/to/ca.pem')`. Node (https): `new https.Agent({ cert: fs.readFileSync('client.crt'), key: fs.readFileSync('client.key'), ca: fs.readFileSync('ca.pem') })` and pass agent to the request. Keep `rejectUnauthorized: true`.

leo: Also check OpenSSL versions — an old OpenSSL in CI can choke on certain chains (ECDSA vs RSA). `openssl s_client -connect api.redwood.example:443 -showcerts` is useful to inspect the chain from inside CI.

infra-bot: Created infra-ticket INFRA-1234 to add a standard step and image tags for CI images that include corporate root certs and docs on env vars.

maria.dev: Awesome — I’ll try the `update-ca-certificates` flow and set `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` as a fallback. If I hit anything weird I’ll paste s_client output here. Thanks everyone :clap:

aj: If you post the `openssl s_client` output I can help interpret the chain. Also if you need a minimal repro I can spin a small container in our testenv with the corp cert added.

maria.dev: Will do.
